problem: "less industrious" rendered "less resourceful" (sense shifted: the point is loss of mental application, but 'industrious' is his word); "laws and manners" here means mores, so style note calls for "customs".
replacement: A workman who spends all his time making one single thing eventually does that work with remarkable skill. At the same time, he loses the general ability to apply his mind to directing the work. Each day he grows more adept and less industrious, so that one may say of him that as the workman improves, the man is degraded. What can be expected of a man who has spent twenty years of his life making heads for pins? And what can that mighty human intelligence, which has so often stirred the world, be used for in him, except to find the best way of making pinheads? When a workman has spent a large part of his life like this, his thoughts are forever fixed on the object of his daily toil. His body has settled into fixed habits that it can never shake off. In a word, he no longer belongs to himself but to the calling he has chosen. It is in vain that laws and customs have taken the trouble to level every barrier around such a man and to open a thousand different roads to fortune before him on every side. A theory of manufactures more powerful than customs and laws ties him to a trade, and often to a place, that he cannot leave. It assigns him a certain position in society, beyond which he cannot go. In the midst of universal movement, it has left him standing still.

problem: Added causal connective "therefore" and dropped the proportional structure ("in proportion as it becomes more manifest").
replacement: The more widely the principle of the division of labor is applied, the weaker, the narrower in mind, and the more dependent the workman becomes. The craft advances; the craftsman falls back. On the other hand, as it becomes more evident that manufactured goods are cheaper and better the larger the manufacture is and the more capital it employs, wealthy and educated men come forward to enter manufactures that used to be left to poor or ignorant craftsmen. The scale of the effort required and the importance of the results to be won attract them. So at the very time that the science of manufactures lowers the class of workmen, it raises the class of masters.

problem: "manners" in the sense of mores (language and manners of a country) should be "customs" per style note.
replacement: Democracy does not attach men strongly to one another, but it puts their everyday dealings on an easier footing. Suppose two Englishmen happen to meet at the Antipodes, surrounded by strangers whose language and customs they hardly know. At first they will stare at each other with great curiosity and a kind of secret uneasiness. Then they will turn away, or, if one speaks to the other, they will take care to talk only about very unimportant subjects, in a constrained and absent manner. Yet there is no enmity between these men; they have never seen each other before, and each believes the other to be respectable. Why, then, do they keep so warily apart? We must go back to England to learn the reason.

problem: "partially by their manners": the sense is mores (shared habits and customs), not politeness; style note calls for "customs".
replacement: In America, privileges of birth have never existed, and wealth gives its owners no special rights. There, men who do not know each other readily frequent the same places and find neither danger nor advantage in freely exchanging their thoughts. If they meet by chance, they neither seek nor avoid conversation. Their manner is therefore natural, frank, and open. It is easy to see that they hardly expect or fear anything from each other, and that they care no more to display than to hide their position in the world. If their demeanor is often cold and serious, it is never haughty or constrained. If they do not talk, it is because they are not in the mood, not because they think it in their interest to keep silent. In a foreign country, two Americans are at once friends, simply because they are Americans. No prejudice repels them; their common country draws them together. For two Englishmen, the same blood is not enough; the same rank must bring them together. The Americans notice this unsociable mood of the English as much as the French do, and are no less astonished by it. Yet the Americans are tied to England by their origin, their religion, their language, and partly by their customs; they differ only in social condition. It may therefore be inferred that the reserve of the English comes much more from the constitution of their country than from that of its inhabitants.

problem: Dropped "eagerly" from "eagerly to seek the company" (nuance).
replacement: The mutual indulgence of the Americans, and the manly confidence with which they treat each other, also result from another, deeper and more general cause, which I already mentioned in the preceding chapter. In the United States, distinctions of rank in civil society are slight, and in political society they are nonexistent. An American therefore does not think himself bound to pay particular attentions to any of his fellow citizens, nor does he require them from others toward himself. Since he does not see that it is in his interest to seek the company of any of his countrymen eagerly, he is slow to imagine that his own company is being refused. He despises no one because of his station, so he does not imagine anyone can despise him for that reason. Until he has clearly perceived an insult, he does not suppose that an affront was intended. The social condition of the Americans naturally accustoms them not to take offense over small matters. And in turn, the democratic freedom they enjoy spreads this same mildness of temper through the character of the nation. The political institutions of the United States constantly bring citizens of all ranks into contact and force them to pursue great undertakings together. People so engaged have hardly time to attend to the details of etiquette, and they also have too strong an interest in living harmoniously to stick at such things. They soon acquire the habit of paying more attention to the feelings and opinions of those they meet than to their manners, and they do not let trifles annoy them.
